title: No. 28 — The Same Subject Continued (The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It cannot be denied that cases may arise in which the national government is compelled to resort to force. Our own experience has confirmed the lessons taught by the examples of other nations: emergencies of this sort will sometimes arise in all societies, however constituted. Seditions and insurrections are, unhappily, maladies as inseparable from the body politic as tumors and eruptions are from the natural body. The idea of governing at all times by the simple force of law, which we have been told is the only admissible principle of republican government, has no place except in the daydreams of those political doctors whose cleverness scorns the lessons of experience.

Should such emergencies ever arise under the national government, there could be no remedy but force. The means used must be proportioned to the extent of the harm. If it were a slight commotion in a small part of a State, the militia of the rest of the State would be adequate to put it down, and the national presumption is that they would be ready to do their duty. An insurrection, whatever its immediate cause, ultimately endangers all government. Concern for the public peace, if not for the rights of the Union, would lead the citizens to whom the contagion had not spread to oppose the insurgents. And if the general government were found in practice to promote the prosperity and happiness of the people, it would be irrational to believe they would be unwilling to support it.

If, on the contrary, the insurrection should spread through a whole State, or a principal part of it, using a different kind of force might become unavoidable. Massachusetts, it appears, found it necessary to raise troops to suppress the disorders within that State, and Pennsylvania, from mere fear of commotions among a part of her citizens, has thought it proper to take the same measure. Suppose the State of New York had been inclined to re-establish her lost jurisdiction over the inhabitants of Vermont. Could she have hoped to succeed in such an enterprise by the efforts of the militia alone? Would she not have been compelled to raise and maintain a more regular force to carry out her design? If it must then be admitted that the necessity of turning to a force other than the militia, in cases of this extraordinary kind, applies to the State governments themselves, why should the possibility that the national government might be under a like necessity in similar extremities be made an objection to its existence? Is it not surprising that men who profess an attachment to the Union in the abstract should urge as an objection to the proposed Constitution what applies with tenfold weight to the plan they advocate, and what, so far as it has any foundation in truth, is an inevitable consequence of civil society on an enlarged scale? Who would not prefer that possibility to the unceasing agitations and frequent revolutions that are the continual scourges of petty republics?

Let us pursue this examination in another light. Suppose that, in place of one general system, two or three or even four Confederacies were formed. Would not the same difficulty stand in the way of the operations of each of these Confederacies? Would not each of them be exposed to the same accidents, and, when these happened, be obliged to resort to the same expedients for upholding its authority that are objected to in a government for all the States? On this supposition, would the militia be any more ready or more able to support the federal authority than in the case of a general union? All fair-minded and intelligent men must, on due consideration, acknowledge that the principle of the objection applies equally to either case. Whether we have one government for all the States, or different governments for different parcels of them, or even an entire separation of the States, there might sometimes be a necessity to use a force constituted differently from the militia, to preserve the peace of the community and to maintain the just authority of the laws against those violent attacks on them that amount to insurrections and rebellions.

Apart from all other reasoning on the subject, it is a full answer to those who demand a more peremptory provision against military establishments in time of peace to say that the whole power of the proposed government is to be in the hands of the representatives of the people. This is the essential security for the rights and privileges of the people, and after all the only effective one, that can be attained in civil society.(1)

If the representatives of the people betray their constituents, nothing is left but to exercise that original right of self-defense, which stands above every positive form of government. Against usurpation by the national rulers, this right can be exercised with infinitely better prospects of success than against usurpation by the rulers of a single State. In a single State, suppose the persons holding supreme power turn usurpers. The parcels, subdivisions, or districts that make up the State have no separate government of their own, so they can take no regular measures for defense. The citizens must rush to arms in confusion, without concert, without system, and with no resources except their courage and despair. The usurpers, clothed with the forms of legal authority, can too often crush the opposition while it is still in its infancy. The smaller the territory, the harder it is for the people to form a regular or systematic plan of opposition, and the easier it is to defeat their first efforts. Word of their preparations and movements reaches the usurpers faster, and the military force in the usurpers' hands can be sent more quickly against the place where the opposition has begun. In this situation, a peculiar combination of circumstances would be needed to bring success to the popular resistance.

As a state grows larger, the obstacles to usurpation grow and the means of resistance multiply, provided the citizens understand their rights and are ready to defend them. In a large community, the people's natural strength compared with the government's artificial strength is greater than in a small one, so the people are better able to contend with the government's attempts to set up a tyranny. But in a confederacy, it is no exaggeration to say that the people are entirely the masters of their own fate. Power is almost always the rival of power, so the general government will always stand ready to check the usurpations of the state governments, and they will be disposed the same way toward the general government. The people, by throwing their weight into either scale, will without fail make it prevail. If either invades their rights, they can use the other as the instrument of redress. How wise it will be for them to cherish the union and so preserve an advantage that can never be valued too highly!

We may safely accept it as an axiom of our political system that, in every possible contingency, the State governments will give complete security against invasions of the public liberty by the national authority. A select body of men is far less likely than the people at large to be taken in by the pretenses under which projects of usurpation are disguised. The legislatures will have better means of information. They can see the danger from a distance. Since they hold all the organs of civil power and have the confidence of the people, they can at once adopt a regular plan of opposition and bring together all the resources of the community. They can easily communicate with one another in the different States and join their common forces to protect their common liberty.

The great size of the country is a further security. We have already seen how useful it was against the attacks of a foreign power, and it would have exactly the same effect against the enterprises of ambitious rulers in the national councils. Suppose the federal army were able to crush the resistance of one State. The distant States would then be able to make a stand with fresh forces. The army would have to give up what it had gained in one place in order to subdue the opposition in others, and the moment the part it had forced into submission was left to itself, its efforts would begin again and its resistance would revive.

We should remember that the size of the military force must in any case be regulated by the resources of the country. For a long time to come it will not be possible to maintain a large army, and as the means of doing so increase, the population and natural strength of the community will increase in proportion. When will the time come that the federal government can raise and maintain an army capable of setting up a despotism over the great body of the people of an immense empire, who are in a position, through their State governments, to take measures for their own defense with all the speed, regularity, and system of independent nations? The fear may be considered a disease for which no cure can be found in the resources of argument and reasoning.
